title: Discourse markers and cohesion
tagline: The right connector shows how two ideas relate — not just that they're next to each other.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (hence, thereby, notwithstanding, such)
Reading & Use of English Part 6 — cross-text cohesion and reference
Writing Part 1 — essay: formal linkers and referencing without repetition
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — natural spoken markers (mind you, anyway, that said)
why: Discourse markers are the glue that turns a list of sentences into a single, coherent argument. At C1 the range widens sharply: formal linkers like albeit, notwithstanding and hence belong in an essay or report; the former/the latter and the above avoid clumsy repetition when referring back to something already said; and a completely different set — mind you, anyway, that said — keeps spoken English natural. Reading & Use of English tests the formal set directly, and examiners reward genuine cohesion, not just a string of linking words, in both Writing tasks.

rows.label: Concession
cells: mind you, it was late / that said, it was late

rows.label: Returning to the point
cells: as previously stated / to return to the point

rows.label: Result
cells: so / that's why it was delayed

diagrams.title: Referring back: the former / the latter
diagrams.caption: Use these only after both things have already been named — never as the first mention.

head: Marker
Function
Example
rows: The project succeeded, albeit later than planned.
Notwithstanding the delays, the bridge opened on schedule.
result, formal, often without a full second clause
The bridge was closed for repairs; hence the diversion.
She rewrote the introduction, thereby clarifying her argument.
The plan is unusual in that it relies entirely on volunteers.
We considered buses and trains; the latter proved cheaper.
referencing a whole idea or category
Persistent absence, and such behaviour, worries every teacher.
The test was hard — mind you, everyone struggled equally.

use.point: Formal linkers of concession and result

examples.text: The scheme was expensive, albeit effective in reducing traffic.
examples.note: albeit + adjective, a very compact concession

examples.text: Notwithstanding some early criticism, the reform is now widely supported.
Attendance fell sharply; hence the school's decision to review the timetable.

use.point: thereby and in that: precise formal connectors

examples.text: The council extended the deadline, thereby giving every team a fair chance.
The essay is unusual in that it argues against its own title.
examples.note: in that = because, introduces an explanation

examples.text: The new bridge reduced journey times, thereby easing pressure on the old road.
examples.note: a result clause in formal register

use.point: Referencing back without repeating: the former/the latter, the above, such

examples.text: The school offers Cambridge and IB routes; the latter suits students planning to study abroad.
examples.note: the latter = the second of two things just mentioned

examples.text: The above figures suggest attendance rises when clubs run after school.
examples.note: the above = what has just been said or shown

examples.text: Constant phone use, poor sleep, missed deadlines — such patterns rarely improve without support.
examples.note: such = referring to a whole category just described

use.point: Spoken markers that keep a conversation natural

examples.text: It was a difficult exam. Mind you, nobody finished it in time either.
examples.note: mind you = adds a contrasting point casually

examples.text: Anyway, as I was saying, the trip is booked for October.
examples.note: anyway = returning to the main topic

examples.text: The film was slow. That said, the ending made it worth watching.
examples.note: that said = a spoken concession, less formal than 'nevertheless'

watch_out.wrong: Albeit the rain, we finished the match.
watch_out.right: We finished the match, albeit in the rain.
watch_out.why: 'Albeit' is followed directly by an adjective, a clause or a short phrase — it doesn't work like 'despite + noun' in every context.

watch_out.wrong: Notwithstanding of the delays, the project succeeded.
watch_out.why: 'Notwithstanding' is followed directly by a noun phrase, with no preposition after it.

watch_out.wrong: The lecture overran, thereby we missed the bus.
watch_out.right: The lecture overran, thereby making us miss the bus.
watch_out.why: 'Thereby' introduces a result with an -ing form, not a new full clause with its own subject.

watch_out.wrong: We discussed grammar and vocabulary; the letter matters more for the exam.
watch_out.right: We discussed grammar and vocabulary; the latter matters more for the exam.
watch_out.why: It's 'the latter' (= the second one mentioned), not 'the letter'.

watch_out.wrong: Such behaviour worry teachers every year.
watch_out.why: 'Such + uncountable/singular noun' takes a singular verb: behaviour worries, not worry.

watch_out.wrong: Mind you that the shop closes early on Sundays.
watch_out.right: Mind you, the shop closes early on Sundays.
watch_out.why: 'Mind you' is a spoken discourse marker that stands alone, followed by a comma — it doesn't take 'that'.

dialogue.title: Two registers, one idea
dialogue.context: Miss Vega compares how Liam and Nadia express the same opinion — one in a spoken discussion, one in a formal essay — to show how discourse markers change with register.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Liam, tell the class what you think about school uniforms — informally, like you would to a friend.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Honestly, uniforms are a bit pointless. Mind you, they do stop arguments about clothes.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. Now, Nadia, give me the same idea in essay style.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: 'Uniforms may seem unnecessary; notwithstanding this, they remove a common source of conflict among students.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Excellent contrast. Liam, what's your final point, casually?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Anyway, most students get used to it after the first term.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: 'Most students adapt within a term; hence, initial objections rarely persist.'

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Can I add something about two schools we compared — the public one and the private one?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: 'We compared the public and the private school; the latter enforces uniform rules far more strictly.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Perfect use of 'the latter'. That said, remember: never mix these two registers in the same paragraph.

items.why: 'albeit' + adjective is a compact way of conceding a point

items.sentence: ___ the criticism, the mayor pressed ahead with the plan.
Ticket sales fell sharply; ___ the decision to cancel the tour.
items.why: 'hence' introduces a result, often without a full second clause

items.sentence: The team rewrote the proposal, ___ addressing every objection raised.
The offer is unusual ___ it requires no deposit at all.
items.why: 'in that' introduces an explanation, similar to 'because'

items.sentence: We can walk or take the bus; ___ takes twice as long.
items.why: 'the latter' refers to the second of two things just mentioned — the bus

items.sentence: The lecture was long. ___, most students stayed until the end.
items.why: a spoken discourse marker adding a contrasting comment

items.sentence: Late arrivals, missed deadlines, forgotten homework — ___ patterns concern every teacher.
items.why: 'such' refers back to a whole category just listed

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one or two words.

items.sentence: The plan was risky, ___ ultimately successful.
___ the setbacks, the charity reached its fundraising target.
The bridge was closed for months; ___ the long detour every morning.
She simplified the instructions, ___ reducing the number of errors.
The offer is generous ___ it covers accommodation as well as travel.
We studied French and German; ___ proved far more useful for her career.
Constant lateness, unfinished homework — ___ habits rarely go unnoticed.
The film dragged in places. ___, the acting was superb.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: The trip was fun, but it was tiring for everyone.
Despite the setbacks, the charity reached its fundraising target.
items.second_end: the charity reached its fundraising target.

items.first: Ticket sales fell sharply, so the tour was cancelled.
She simplified the instructions, and this reduced the number of errors.
The offer is generous because it covers accommodation as well as travel.
items.second_end: it covers accommodation as well as travel.

items.first: We studied French and German; German proved far more useful for her career.
items.second_end: proved far more useful for her career.

summary: Formal linkers like albeit, notwithstanding, hence and thereby belong in essays and reports; keep mind you, anyway and that said for speech.
The former/the latter, the above and such refer back to something already mentioned, without clumsy repetition.
In that introduces an explanation (= because); thereby introduces a result, usually with an -ing verb.
Real cohesion is more than linking words: repeating a key idea with a synonym ties a paragraph together as much as any connector does.
Never mix registers in the same paragraph — a formal essay with 'anyway' in it, or a conversation full of 'notwithstanding', both sound wrong.
